title: The Noise That Doesn't Turn Off
audioPath: support-audios/Anxiety Relief/The Noise That Doesn't Turn Off.mp3
thumbPath: support-audio-thumbs/Anxiety Relief/The Noise That Doesn't Turn Off.png
transcript: You know there's nothing wrong. Not really. And your chest is tight anyway. Your mind's already three steps ahead, rehearsing conversations that haven't happened, building arguments for problems that don't exist yet. That's anxiety. Not the "I'm a little nervous" kind everyone experiences sometimes. The kind that doesn't need a reason to show up. It just arrives. And once it does, it doesn't seem to care that you know logically that you're safe. Your nervous system is running a threat detection system that's a little too generous with what counts as a threat. An email, a silence in a conversation, a thought that crossed your mind at 2:00 AM. None of it is dangerous, but your body doesn't always get that memo in time. And if you've been carrying this a while, you've probably learned to hide it well, function through it, smile through it. That takes something out of you that most people never see. So what actually helps? Not "Just calm down." If that worked, you'd have done it already. It's learning to notice the spiral starting before it takes you all the way up. A tight chest, racing thoughts. That's the early signal, not the emergency itself. Small things. One slow breath. Naming what you're feeling out loud. Putting your feet flat on the ground. They don't fix anxiety, but they interrupt it. Sometimes that's enough for a moment. And if this is more than a passing wave for you, if it's most days, most hours, that's worth saying out loud to someone. A therapist, a doctor, someone who can actually help carry it. You're not broken for feeling this. You're just tired of carrying something loud alone.

title: Too Many Small Doors
transcript: What to wear, what to eat, which email to answer first. By two PM, you can't even decide what you want for lunch, and it's not because the decision is hard. It's a sandwich. It shouldn't take this much out of you, but it does. That's decision fatigue. And here's the part that surprises people. It has nothing to do with how smart you are or how capable. It's about volume. Your brain treats every choice, big or small, as a trainee withdrawal from the same account. What to wear, what to say back, which task to start first. None of them cost much on their own, but by the end of the day, that account is running on empty. And the last decisions you make are always the worst ones, which is why you end up eating the same thing you always eat, or snapping at someone over something small, or just standing in front of the fridge, unable to choose anything at all. That's not a character flaw. That's just what a depleted brain does. So what actually helps? Not more discipline. You don't need to want to decide better. It's removing decisions you don't need to be making in the first place. The same breakfast most days, clothes picked the night before. One less thing to negotiate with yourself about. Save your real decisions for when you actually have something left to decide with. You're not indecisive. You're just out of decisions for today, and that's allowed.

title: The Flatness No One Warned You About
audioPath: support-audios/Depression (Non-Crisis)/The Flatness No One Warned You About.mp3
transcript: Nothing's technically wrong. You're not crying. You're not falling apart. You're just gray, like someone turned the color down on everything. Food doesn't taste like much. Things you used to enjoy just feel like effort now. Not sad exactly, just flat. That's depression too. Even without the version everyone pictures, the dramatic collapse, the visible tears. This kind is quieter, harder to name, easier to miss. It's not really about sadness. It's about a kind of numbness, a loss of interest in things that used to pull you in. Low energy that sleep doesn't fix. A sense that you're just going through the motions of your own life. And because it doesn't look like a crisis, people, including you, often just call it being tired, being busy, needing a break. Sometimes it's none of those things. Sometimes it's this. If this sounds familiar, I want to say something plainly. You don't need to be in crisis for this to be worth taking seriously. You don't have to wait until it gets unbearable before it counts. So what actually helps? Not forcing yourself to feel grateful. Not just get outside more. Though movement can help, it isn't a fix on its own. It's naming it first. Saying, even just to yourself, "I think this is more than tired." And letting that be enough reason to talk to someone. A doctor, a therapist, someone trained to help carry this kind of weight, not just witness it. You don't have to earn the right to ask for help. Flat isn't fine. It's just quiet. And quiet still deserves attention.

title: The Loss That Doesn't Get a Card
audioPath: support-audios/Grief/The Loss That Doesn't Get a Card.mp3
transcript: Nobody sent flowers. Nobody asked how you're doing. Because on paper, nothing died. But something ended. A friendship that just stopped without an explanation. A version of your life you thought you'd have. A relationship that's technically still there but isn't what it was anymore. That's grief too. Even without a funeral, even without a name people recognize. Grief isn't really about death, not at its core. It's about loss, the end of something you were attached to, whether the world agrees it was significant or not. And when there's no ceremony for it, no one bringing food, no one saying, "I'm sorry for your loss," it can feel like you're not even allowed to grieve it. Like you have to just get over something nobody agreed was worth grieving in the first place. You are allowed. This counts. The friendship that faded, the dream that quietly closed, the parent who's still alive but isn't who they were, the body that used to work differently. All of it is loss. All of it deserves space. So what actually helps? Not rushing to feel better, not comparing your loss to someone else's, deciding yours doesn't measure up. It's letting yourself name it as grief out loud, even if no one else calls it that. Grief without a ritual still needs somewhere to go. Write it down. Say it to one person who won't minimize it. Light a candle for something that has no headstone. You don't need permission to mourn something real. Not everything that ends gets a funeral, but everything that mattered deserves to be grieved.

title: Running on a Tank You Didn't Refill
audioPath: support-audios/Mild Burnout/Running on a Tank You Didn't Refill.mp3
transcript: You're not sick. You're not sad exactly. You're just done, and you can't remember the last day you didn't feel that way. That flatness has a name, even if it doesn't always get taken seriously. Burnout. Not the dramatic quit your job kind people picture. The quieter kind. The kind that creeps in slowly enough that you almost don't notice it arriving. Burnout researchers describe it as a mix of three things. Exhaustion that rest doesn't fix, a growing distance from things you used to care about, and a nagging sense that nothing you do really matters anyway. It's not the same as being tired. Tired goes away with sleep. This doesn't. And because it builds so slowly, most people don't catch it until they're already deep in it. So what actually helps? Not a vacation. Vacations end. This doesn't. The first step isn't fixing it. It's just recognizing it. Honestly, no performance. Ask yourself, when did you last feel like yourself doing something you actually used to enjoy? If the answer is 'I can't remember,' that's information, not failure. Naming it isn't giving up. It's the first honest thing you've done about it in a while.

title: The Weight You Didn't Notice You Were Carrying
audioPath: support-audios/Mild Stress/The Weight You Didn't Notice You Were Carrying.mp3
transcript: Your jaw's tight, your shoulders are up by your ears, and you didn't even notice until just now. That's mild stress, the kind that doesn't announce itself. No crisis, no big moment, just tension quietly building in the background of an ordinary day. Here's the thing about mild stress: it's not the enemy. A little bit of it is just your body responding to normal demands. A deadline, a full inbox, too many small decisions before noon. The problem isn't that it shows up. The problem is when it never fully leaves. Because stress that doesn't get released just stacks. One tight shoulders day becomes a tight shoulders week. And most people don't notice the buildup. They just start calling it normal. So what actually helps? Not a vacation, not just relax. It's noticing the signal early. The jaw, the shoulders, the shallow breathing, and doing something small about it right then, not later, not after the to-do list is done. Try this. Right now, drop your shoulders. Unclench your jaw. Take one slow breath all the way down. That's it. That's the whole intervention sometimes. Small, repeated, on time. Not one big reset at the end of the week. Your body's been holding on to something. You're allowed to put it down, even for a few seconds.

title: The Procrastination Trap
transcript: You know the assignment's due tomorrow. You know exactly what to do, and somehow you're bed rotting instead. That's procrastination, and if you've spent your life calling it laziness, here's some good news. It's probably not. Procrastination isn't usually about the task itself. It's about the feeling the task brings up. Researchers who study procrastination describe it less as a time management problem and more as an emotion management problem. When a task feels boring, overwhelming, or tied to fear of failing, your brain looks for relief, and relief is one click away. Bed rotting isn't the point. It's just easier than the discomfort. And here's the trap. The relief is real, but it's short. The task is still there. Now it's closer, and so is the deadline. That's why procrastination so often ends in a late night, fueled by panic instead of choice. So what actually helps? It's not more willpower. It's making the task feel less threatening. Try shrinking it. Not write the report. Open the document and write one sentence. Momentum tends to follow action, not the other way around. And if the avoidance is about fear, fear of doing it badly, it helps to say that part out loud, even just to yourself. "I'm avoiding this because I'm scared it won't be good enough." Naming the real reason often loosens its grip. You don't have to feel ready to start. You just have to start, smaller than you think you need to.

title: Fine, on Paper
transcript: Nobody yelled. Nobody left. But something's different, and you can't quite point to when it started. You still talk, you still share a life, but it feels more like coexisting than actually being together. That's relationship strain, and it rarely arrives as one big rupture. It's slower than that, quieter. It's the conversations that used to run long now running short, the inside jokes that don't come up as often, the small check-ins that used to happen without thinking now requiring effort.
